### Observed differences

- The dominant change is a reversal of execution order between two groups of activities. In the earlier window, A20, A21, A22, A24 and A25 — each present in essentially every trace — sat at about 39–40% of the trace's event positions, while A19, A23, A26, A27 and A28 — each in roughly one in five traces — sat at about 69–72%. In the later window these positions are exchanged: the first group at about 64%, the second at about 32–36%. [POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, POS005, POS006, POS007, POS008, POS009, POS010]
- The pairwise order relations flip accordingly. Earlier, A20–A25 preceded A29 in about 99 in 100 co-occurring traces and preceded A33 in about 98 in 100; later, A29 and A33 precede them in about 98–99 in 100. [REL004, REL005, REL009, REL010, REL014, REL015, REL021, REL022, REL025, REL026]
- The same flip holds between the two groups: earlier, A20–A25 preceded A23, A27 and A28 in nearly every trace where both occurred (these pairs co-occur in about 19–25 in 100 traces); later the order is reversed with almost identical frequencies. [REL001, REL002, REL003, REL006, REL007, REL008, REL011, REL012, REL013, REL016, REL017, REL019, REL023]
- The occasional activities' relation to A29 and A33 also reversed: earlier A29/A33 preceded A23, A27 and A28 (about 20–24 in 100 traces); later A23/A27/A28 precede A29/A33. [REL018, REL027, REL028, REL029, REL030]
- Outgoing transitions at the group boundaries changed hands. Earlier, A19, A23, A26, A27 and A28 led almost exclusively to A34 (about 89–98 in 100 outgoing transitions); later they lead to A29 (about 92–100 in 100). Earlier, A20–A25 sent about 15–29 in 100 of their outgoing transitions to A29 and essentially none to A34; later that share goes to A34 (about 18–22 in 100) and A29 is no longer a successor. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004, DIR005, DIR006, DIR007, DIR008, DIR009, DIR010]
- A33 and A44 now feed the other group: A33's outgoing transitions pointed mainly to A26, A19, A23, A28 and A27 earlier, and to A24, A22, A25, A20 and A21 later; A44 pointed into the A20–A25 group earlier and into the A19/A23/A26–A28 group later. [DIR011, DIR012]
- Short-distance patterns mirror this. Earlier, A33 was followed by A34 within two steps in about 193 of 200 traces, and A27 and A28 immediately preceded A34 (about 46 and 45 traces); later, A20 and A21 are followed by A34 within five steps in about 190 of 200 traces, A26 immediately precedes A29 (36 traces), and A44 immediately precedes A26 in about 31 of 36 traces. [LAG001, LAG002, LAG003, LAG004, LAG005, LAG009, LAG010, LAG011, LAG012]
- Participation is essentially unchanged: A20–A25, A29 and A33 occur in about all traces in both windows, and A19/A23/A26–A28 in about 17–27 in 100 in both. A29 (mean position about 0.49 → 0.37) and A33 (about 0.67 → 0.55) moved earlier but kept their relative order. The change is therefore a reordering of existing behaviour, not activities appearing, disappearing or changing how often they run. [POS001, POS005, POS008, POS009, POS010, POS011, POS012]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that two blocks of activities exchanged their place in the flow. In the earlier window, A44 was followed by the always-present block A20, A21, A22, A24, A25, then A29, then A33, then one of the occasional activities A19, A23, A26, A27, A28, which led to A34; in the later window, A44 is followed by the occasional activity, then A29, then A33, then the A20–A25 block, which leads to A34. A29 and A33 kept their relative order but moved earlier along with the block that now precedes them. Supporting signs: the order reversals are near-deterministic in both directions (about 98–99.5 in 100 co-occurring traces), the position shifts match the reversal in size and direction, the successor changes sit exactly at the block boundaries, and participation shares are unchanged, which rules out path replacement or activities becoming optional, mandatory or repeated differently. The screening context also fits: 66 qualifying items against fewer than 1 expected without change, although many items describe the same underlying swap and are not independent confirmations. Limitations: positions and lags are measured in event positions rather than clock time, several lag profiles rest on a single observation in one window (so exact distances, such as A33–A34 within two steps, are indicative only), and the indicators cannot show whether every trace reversed uniformly or the mix of trace variants shifted, nor what happens before A44 or after A34. [REL004, REL014, REL001, REL016, REL027, POS002, POS005, POS011, DIR005, DIR007, DIR011, LAG003, LAG010]

Other differences: a few low-share outgoing transitions appeared in the later window — A19 to A38, A35 and A14, and A23 to A27, each about 3 in 100 — and A19's position spread widened; these are peripheral to the block exchange. [DIR001, DIR005, POS001]
